parts.title: The Longest Conservation Fence In The World
parts.article:
(A) When a wooden post was hammered into a path of Kenyan soil on 28 August 2009, it marked the completion of the longest conservation fence in the world. The 400-kilometre-long, two-metre-high electrified barrier, which protects more than 2,000 square kilometres of lush, green rainforest, took more than 20 years to construct. It was originally built by an animal conservation charity to conserve the black rhino – an endangered species of rhino whose numbers in the region had fallen from hundreds to dozens. However, its effects and beneficiaries have proved to be considerably more wide-ranging.

(B) The fence encircles part of the Aberdare mountains, a 160-kilometre-long range that forms the eastern rim of the Great Rift Valley just north of the capital Nairobi. Well loved by safari-goers, it's a water-rich region that contains a mixture of habitats, including rainforest, bamboo forest and moorland. But its wildlife had been suffering as Nairobi's growing population crept up into the highlands to farm its volcanic soils. Kenya's population has grown from about three million at the start of the 20th century to around 40 million today, and although many have migrated into the country's cities, about three quarters of Kenyans still live off the land. But unfortunately, Kenya doesn't have much fertile land. Vast areas of the country are little more than desert, and only around 17 per cent is suitable for farming. As people moved up into the Aberdares' forests the region became degraded, as trees were felled for firewood or to make way for farming and cattle grazing, and local wildlife was hunted.

(C) Various government and conservation organisations had tried to halt the destruction, but it was difficult to stop illegal uses of the forest, including poaching – the unlawful hunting of animals – when there was no barrier to prevent entry. 'One of the problems was that people couldn't really tell where the state-owned, out-of-bounds area began,' explains Colin Church, the chairman of the animal conservation charity. 'We needed to communicate to local people which land was theirs and which was for the benefit of all Kenyans.'

(D) Initially, there were concerns that the fence would be rejected by the people living in the nearby area, who had become accustomed to supplementing their income with the forest's resources. However, that doesn't seem to have been the case. 'When we were carrying out the assessments, we held five meetings with fence-adjacent communities and most of them were very happy with the fence,' says Professor David Mungai of the University of Nairobi, who led the team that prepared a report on the fence's impact.

(E) It soon became clear that the fence has been welcomed because it doesn't just protect animals from people, it also protects people from animals. Before it was built, farmers near the forests would regularly lose a substantial proportion of their harvest to marauding wild animals, and children were often attacked on their way to school by predators. 'In this situation, it was difficult for those living near the fence to care too much about conserving the area and its wildlife,' says Church. But the fence has changed that relationship. Since its construction, the 40,000 farmers whose lands border the fence have gained considerably. 'Most are now able to harvest 100 per cent of their crops,' says Church. The improved security has seen land values increase by up to 300 per cent, and poaching is down by 99 per cent, according to Dr Julius Kipng'etich, Director of the Kenya Wildlife Service.

(F) Further local support has been secured by hiring local people to build the fence and act as its guardians – living in specially created cabins beside the fence and patrolling sections up to 20 kilometres in length on a daily basis. 'The fence isn't possible without the support of the local community,' says Mungai. He believes that the increased support of local people – many of whom are under-educated and unemployed – will be secured through government investment in schools and job creation, including the setting up of more ecotourism businesses. The area currently receives around 50,000 visitors a year, but there is a widespread view that its tourism potential remains relatively untapped.

(G) As the region's forests start to recover – reports show that indigenous forest cover within the enclosure has increased by 20 per cent – its rivers have also started to stabilize. 'If you remove an area's vegetation, the troughs and peaks of water flow are increased – so the base flow becomes lower, and flooding and erosion become an issue,' says Mungai. 'What's important is that a river is stable, so the local people can trust in what that river will be able to deliver.' Colin Church also sees the Aberdare fence as a true success story. 'The conservation struggle is so often presented as man versus nature. But with the right management, that doesn't need to be the case,' he says. 'The two can benefit each other and live sustainably side by side. We've proved it.'

(H) The success of the Aberdare fence has attracted international attention. Conservationists from other African countries, as well as from Asia and South America, have visited the site to learn from the experience. The key lesson, according to Church, is that conservation must work with local communities, not against them. 'Too many conservation projects fail because they try to exclude people,' he says. 'But people are part of the ecosystem. If they don't benefit from protecting nature, they will have no reason to protect it.' The fence model is now being considered for other sensitive habitats, including national parks in Tanzania and wildlife corridors in India.

(I) Looking ahead, the challenge will be to maintain the fence and the goodwill it has generated. The electrified barrier requires regular maintenance, and the guardians need ongoing support and training. Climate change poses a new threat, with more erratic rainfall potentially affecting both the forest and the farms that depend on it. Yet the project's founders remain optimistic. 'We've shown that it's possible to balance human needs with conservation,' says Mungai. 'The fence is just a tool. The real achievement is the change in people's attitudes.'

Questions 18 and 19

Q18 According to the text, which TWO benefits of the fence have been observed?

  • A an improvement in soil quality
  • B a more reliable water supply
  • C growth in tourism
  • D larger harvests
  • E increased opportunities for research

Q19 According to the text, which TWO benefits of the fence have been observed?

Questions 20–24
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2?
In boxes 20–24 on your answer sheet, write:

Q20 The fence took more than two decades to complete.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q21 Less than 10 per cent of Kenya's land is suitable for farming.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q22 Local communities were initially opposed to the construction of the fence.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q23 Children were sometimes attacked by wild animals before the fence was built.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q24 The fence has eliminated all conflict between humans and wildlife in the region.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 25–26
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Write your answers in boxes 25–26 on your answer sheet.

Q25 What does Colin Church identify as the main reason for the failure of many conservation projects?

  • A lack of funding from international donors
  • B opposition from local communities
  • C trying to exclude people from conservation areas
  • D poor design of conservation barriers

Q26 What new challenge does the passage mention for the future of the Aberdare region?

  • A declining interest from tourists
  • B climate change affecting rainfall patterns
  • C increasing poaching despite the fence
  • D government cuts to conservation funding

reference:
Q14

解析 题目中说栅栏是为了保护一种罕见的什么，原文对应说它最初被建起来是为了保护黑犀牛（black rhino），也就是一种濒危的犀牛。

干扰 你可能想填black，但题目要求只能填一个词，而且题目里的“a rare type of（一种罕见的）”对应的就是原文的“an endangered species of（一种濒危的）”，后面紧跟的核心名词是rhino。

句子 The 400-kilometre-long, two-metre-high electrified barrier, which protects more than 2,000 square kilometres of lush, green rainforest, took more than 20 years to construct. It was originally built by an animal conservation charity to conserve the black rhino – an endangered species of rhino whose numbers in the region had fallen from hundreds to dozens.

Q15

解析 题目问树木被砍伐用来做什么，原文明确说到树木被砍伐（felled）是为了用来做柴火（firewood）。

干扰 你可能会受句子后半部分影响想填farming，但原文中farming前有“make way for（为...腾出地方）”，表示砍树是为了腾出空地种田，而不是把树木本身“用作”种田。

句子 As people moved up into the Aberdares' forests the region became degraded, as trees were felled for firewood or to make way for farming and cattle grazing, and local wildlife was hunted.

Q16

解析 题目问肯尼亚野生动物服务局局长表示建了栅栏后什么东西大幅减少了，原文中局长的话指出“poaching（偷猎）”下降了99%。

干扰 题目问的是“reduction（减少）”，而在原文这句里，土地价值（land values）是上升（increase）的，只有偷猎（poaching）是下降的。

句子 The improved security has seen land values increase by up to 300 per cent, and poaching is down by 99 per cent, according to Dr Julius Kipng'etich, Director of the Kenya Wildlife Service.

Q17

解析 题目问栅栏的持续成功取决于谁在教育和工作上花钱，原文中Mungai教授指出这要通过“government（政府）”在学校和创造就业上的投资来实现。

干扰 你可能会顺着前文提到的人群想填local people（当地人），但原文强调的是通过“政府投资（government investment）”来获得当地人的支持，真正出钱的主体是政府。

句子 'The fence isn't possible without the support of the local community,' says Mungai. He believes that the increased support of local people – many of whom are under-educated and unemployed – will be secured through government investment in schools and job creation, including the setting up of more ecotourism businesses.

Q18

解析 题目问栅栏带来了什么好处，原文提到随着森林恢复，河流也开始稳定，当地人可以信赖河流能持续提供的水量，这完美对应选项B中的“更可靠的水源供应”。

干扰 你可能会看错选A或C；原文虽然提到了火山土壤，但没说土壤质量变好了；原文也提到旅游业，但说的是潜力“未被开发（untapped）”，而不是旅游业已经获得了增长（选项C）。

句子 As the region's forests start to recover – reports show that indigenous forest cover within the enclosure has increased by 20 per cent – its rivers have also started to stabilize. 'If you remove an area's vegetation, the troughs and peaks of water flow are increased – so the base flow becomes lower, and flooding and erosion become an issue,' says Mungai. 'What's important is that a river is stable, so the local people can trust in what that river will be able to deliver.'

Q19

解析 原文明确提到栅栏建好改变了野生动物破坏庄稼的局面，大多数农民现在能“收获100%的农作物（harvest 100 per cent of their crops）”，对应选项D的“更大的丰收”。

干扰 你可能想选E，但原文通篇都没有提及栅栏的建设增加了任何供研究的机会（opportunities for research），属于完全无中生有的干扰项。

句子 But the fence has changed that relationship. Since its construction, the 40,000 farmers whose lands border the fence have gained considerably. 'Most are now able to harvest 100 per cent of their crops,' says Church.

Q20

解析 题目说建栅栏花了二十多年（more than two decades），原文明确表示建造花去了20多年（more than 20 years），意思完全一致。

干扰 此处只需知道two decades就是20年，属于简单的同义替换，不要因为没看到数字而犹豫。

句子 The 400-kilometre-long, two-metre-high electrified barrier, which protects more than 2,000 square kilometres of lush, green rainforest, took more than 20 years to construct.

Q21

解析 题目说只有不到10%（Less than 10 per cent）的土地适合务农，但原文给出的真实数据是大约17%（around 17 per cent）适合务农，数据矛盾。

干扰 做判断题时遇到数字要格外敏感，17%大于10%，两者直接冲突，所以选FALSE。

句子 Vast areas of the country are little more than desert, and only around 17 per cent is suitable for farming.

Q22

解析 题目说当地社区最初反对建栅栏，但原文明确表示实际上当地社区“对栅栏非常满意（very happy with the fence）”，两者意思完全相反。

干扰 你可能会因为看到原文第一句出现了“concerns（担忧）”和“rejected（拒绝）”就匆忙选TRUE，但紧接着的第15句用“However”反转并澄清了这并不是事实。

句子 Initially, there were concerns that the fence would be rejected by the people living in the nearby area, who had become accustomed to supplementing their income with the forest's resources. However, that doesn't seem to have been the case. 'When we were carrying out the assessments, we held five meetings with fence-adjacent communities and most of them were very happy with the fence,' says Professor David Mungai...

Q23

解析 题目说建栅栏前孩子们有时会被野生动物袭击，原文清楚地写到孩子们在去学校的路上经常被捕食者袭击（attacked... by predators），表述一致。

干扰 只要定位到“children”和“attacked”，确认时间状语“Before it was built”与题干一致，这道题基本不会错。

句子 Before it was built, farmers near the forests would regularly lose a substantial proportion of their harvest to marauding wild animals, and children were often attacked on their way to school by predators.

Q24

解析 题目说栅栏消除了人类和野生动物之间的“所有（all）”冲突，但原文只提到偷猎行为下降了99%（down by 99 per cent），说明并没有百分之百完全消除，两者矛盾。

干扰 在做判断题时，看到题目中的绝对化词汇“all（所有的）”要特别警惕，原文99%的数据细节决定了这题是FALSE而不是NOT GIVEN。

句子 The improved security has seen land values increase by up to 300 per cent, and poaching is down by 99 per cent, according to Dr Julius Kipng'etich, Director of the Kenya Wildlife Service.

Q25

解析 题目问Colin Church认为许多保护项目失败的主要原因是什么，原文中他直接指出是因为这些项目试图“把人们排除在外（exclude people）”，对应选项C。

干扰 你可能会凭常识去猜想是缺乏资金或遭到当地反对，但做阅读题必须严格遵循原文，原文唯一提到的失败原因就是没有让当地人参与进来。

句子 The key lesson, according to Church, is that conservation must work with local communities, not against them. 'Too many conservation projects fail because they try to exclude people,' he says.

Q26

解析 题目问文章提到了该地区未来面临的什么新挑战，原文明确指出“气候变化构成了一个新威胁（Climate change poses a new threat）”，会导致降雨不规律，对应选项B。

干扰 其他选项如旅游兴趣下降、偷猎增加或政府削减资金，在原文讨论未来挑战的最后一段中根本没有出现过，看到Climate change直接锁定答案即可。

句子 Climate change poses a new threat, with more erratic rainfall potentially affecting both the forest and the farms that depend on it.
